conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the evidence supports the efficacy of EMDR therapy in alleviating PTSD symptoms, citing multiple meta-analyses and clinical guidelines from major health organizations. Therefore, it strongly endorses the claim.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
The evidence does not support "no" — the research base actually indicates EMDR **does** help alleviate PTSD symptoms.

Multiple meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials converge on this conclusion. A 2014 quantitative meta-analysis of 26 RCTs (1991–2013) published in PLOS ONE found EMDR therapy effective for PTSD (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0103676). A more recent 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis (covering trials from 1991–2022) similarly concluded EMDR is efficacious for treating PTSD symptoms (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37882423/). Other systematic reviews summarized on Wikipedia note that since 2013, EMDR's efficacy for adult PTSD has generally been found equivalent to established trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapies (CBT), including prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_movement_desensitization_and_reprocessing).

This body of evidence is also reflected in major clinical guidelines. The World Health Organization's mhGAP guidelines explicitly recommend EMDR alongside trauma-focused CBT for adults with PTSD (https://www.who.int/teams/mental-health-and-substance-use/treatment-care/mental-health-gap-action-programme/evidence-centre/conditions-related-to-stress/posttraumatic-stress-disorder-(ptsd)--psychological-interventions---adults). The American Psychological Association's 2017 Clinical Practice Guideline gives EMDR a "conditional" recommendation—weaker than its top-tier recommendations for CBT variants, but still an endorsement of demonstrated benefit rather than a rejection of efficacy (https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/treatments).

**Conclusion:** The weight of evidence from RCT meta-analyses and international clinical guidelines (WHO, APA) supports that EMDR can alleviate PTSD symptoms, generally performing comparably to established trauma-focused therapies. The correct answer to the question is "yes," not "no."
